text:
Discussing Solutions and Strategies

Have students share their thoughts on the relationship between radius squares and the are of a circle. Have students share their thoughts on the relationship between the area of the parallelogram and the circle in What If . . . ? Situation A. Have groups share their solutions and strategies for What If . . . ? Situation B. This could be done with a gallery walk to begin the conversation if during the Explore the students put their work on larger paper. (Portrayal)

Making the Mathematics Explicit

Have students describe the area formula for a circle in relation to radius squares. Their informal language alongside the symbols will assist students in solidifying their understanding of the area formula for a circle. (Language)

Students should see that the circumference of the circle is approximately twice the length of the base of the parallelogram (or the base of the parallelogram is half the circumference of the circle) and the height of the parallelogram is the length of the radius of the circle.

Suggested Questions:

  • How did you find the area of the circles in the Initial Challenge?

This is a conversation on the Initial Challenge from one classroom:

Teacher: How did you find the area of the circles in the Initial Challenge?

Remi: We counted the full squares and created squares out of the other pieces. (Remi demonstrates this by showing their work on the document camera.)

Hensley: We started out like that, but then we kept getting mixed up.

We decided to try Yolanda’s idea. We cut each circle into radius squares. Each time, we saw that 4 radius squares were too much, so the area would be between 3 and 4 radius squares. We counted 1 square and then multiplied that by 3.5 to get the full area.

Teacher: Why did you multiply by 3.5?

Hensley: We weren’t sure exactly how many, but we knew 4 was too much and 3 was too small.

Remi: If you use 3.5, that is too much. It is a lot more than when we counted the squares.

Teacher: What do other people think?

Lily: I think what Hensley’s group did to start this is a great idea because cutting up the whole thing and counting all those pieces of squares is frustrating. I just think 3.5 is too much. It doesn’t look like 3.5 squares too me. I think it is much less than 3.5 squares to cover the circle.

Hensley: Yeah. We thought it was a little big too, but it was closer than 4 radius squares.

Remi: Hensley’s group and my group all found the area using the number of squares to cover the circle. We just found the number of squares using different strategies.

Hensley: Wait a minute. What if it is π number of radius squares?

Remi: What?

Hensley: Yeah. If π is a little more than 3, then this might be how many radius squares cover the circle.

There was a lot of murmuring among the groups. So the teacher gave the students time to turn and talk to their groups about this conjecture.

Teacher: Can we generalize this idea with a formula?

Lily: r2 represents finding the area of the radius square, and then 3.1 is what we used for π , so we could write A = π r2.

• How many radius squares did it take to cover the circles in the Initial Challenge? (Answers will vary. Their answers should be a little more than three radius circles.)

Discuss pi, and have students describe how A = π r2 is related to their work in the Initial Challenge.

  • How does the area of the “parallelogram” compare to the area of the circle in What If . . . ? Situation A? (Answers will vary. The circumference of the circle is about twice the length of the base of the “parallelogram,” and the height of the “parallelogram” is the length of the radius of the circle.)
  • How would the accuracy of your answer change if you cut the pizza into more slices? (If you cut the pizza into more slices, then the parallelogram looks closer to a rectangle. That means the height of the parallelogram is close to the radius of the circle.)

If groups put What If . . . ? Situation B on large paper, have students do a gallery walk. Using sticky notes, have students first go to posters that did the same situation their group did and put sticky note questions on posters. Then have students go to another poster of a situation they didn’t work on. Using a sticky note, decide if they agree or disagree with the group and why or why not.

During the gallery walk, as a teacher, look for the sticky notes that will generate discussions around area and/or circumference of a circle. Look for the situations that students are unsure of or in disagreement about so that the discussion can work on misconceptions or errors. (Language)

Now What Do Students Know

Ask students to reflect on the discussion and answer the Now What Do You Know? questions.

See answers to the problem for more information about the strategies and embedded mathematics.

Reflecting on Student Learning  

Use the following questions to assess student understanding at the end of the lesson.  

• What evidence do I have that students understand the Now What Do You Know? question?

  • Where did my students get stuck?
  • What strategies did they use?
  • What breakthroughs did my students have today?

• How will I use this to plan for tomorrow? For the next time I teach this lesson?

• Where will I have the opportunity to reinforce these ideas as I continue through this unit? The next unit?
